content: The studies were categorized based on the income classification of the country (high-income countries [HIC] versus lowand middle-income countries [LMIC]), the anaemia status of participants at the start of the intervention (anaemic, non-anaemic, or unknown anaemia status as defined by the trialists), and the type of sponsor (industry versus academic investigator). Sensitivity analyses were conducted where possible to assess the potential effects of clustering on the confidence intervals (CIs) of summary estimates. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Each outcome was assessed based on the following GRADE criteria: risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. In 2021, a total of 15,496 unique records were identified through database searches. After removing duplicates, 8,313 records were screened based on titles and abstracts. Most records were excluded as they did not meet the inclusion criteria. A total of 494 full-text records were assessed for eligibility, with 21 studies meeting the inclusion criteria (16 studies with full-text publications and 5 studies with unpublished results). For details on the included trials, refer to Appendix 2. The included studies involved 5,089 participants. Eight studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) at the individual level, one was a non-randomized controlled trial, and seven were cluster-RCTs. Only one study was conducted in a high-income country (USA), while the majority were conducted in upper-middle-income countries (e.g., China, Brazil, Thailand, Mexico, South Africa, Guatemala) and lower-middle-income countries (e.g., Zambia, Cameroon, India, Ghana). No studies were conducted in low-income countries. The age of participants ranged from 6 to 60 months, and all studies included children of both sexes. Sample sizes varied from 40 participants in one study to 1,465 in another. Analyses included only participants allocated to study arms relevant to the systematic review. For cluster-randomized trials, effective sample sizes were adjusted to account for clustering effects. Baseline anaemia prevalence was reported in nine studies. Two studies included only anaemic or moderately anaemic participants, while seven studies included both anaemic and non-anaemic children. Baseline anaemia status was not reported in the remaining seven studies. Intervention durations varied widely, from acute studies lasting three feeding sessions to longer-term studies lasting up to 18 months. Most fortified products were cereals, including wheat-based, maize/corn-based, rice-based, and pearl millet products. Some studies used cereal-legume blends or fortified legumes. Fortification included iron alone in six studies, while others used combinations of micronutrients such as iron, zinc, vitamin A, and B vitamins. Biofortification was employed in two studies. Primary outcomes measured included growth (weight-for-age Z-scores, weight-for-height/length Z-scores, height/length-for-age Z-scores), nutrient adequacy (zinc and vitamin A), anaemia, haemoglobin concentrations, iron status (ferritin, body iron, free erythrocyte porphyrin), and serum retinol and zinc concentrations. Secondary outcomes included mental and motor skill development, morbidity (e.g., diarrhoea, respiratory diseases), plasma vitamin E concentrations, and acceptability of fortified versus non-fortified foods. Adverse effects were reported in one study. No studies reported on stunting, wasting, nutrient excess, all-cause mortality, gut microbiota composition, or food displacement. Funding sources varied, with eight studies funded by government or non-commercial organizations, six studies funded partially or fully by commercial entities, and two studies not reporting funding sources. Five ongoing trials were identified but not yet published as full-text articles. Risk of bias was assessed for all included studies. Randomization processes were appropriately described in only two studies, while concerns were noted in others due to insufficient information or issues with allocation sequence concealment. Deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, and measurement or reporting biases were also noted in several studies. Cluster-randomized trials and crossover trials were evaluated for additional risks, such as timing of participant recruitment and carryover effects. Overall, 50% of the studies were rated as having a high risk of bias due to issues with randomization, deviations from intended interventions, or missing outcome data. Most studies focused on anaemia and haematological indices, with fewer reporting on growth and developmental outcomes. Twelve studies provided data for quantitative analyses, while others were summarized narratively. No significant differences were detected between fortified and non-fortified complementary food groups in terms of primary outcomes. Nutrient intakes above the tolerable upper intake level were not reported in any study.
